exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 17–26, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer. Here $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$B = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ is a basis for a subspace $$H$$ and if $$\textbf{x} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p},$$ then $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ are the coordinates of $$\textbf{x}$$ relative to the basis $$B$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$B$$ is a basis for a subspace $$H,$$ then each vector in $$H$$ can be written in only one way as a linear combination of the vectors in $$B$$ .﻿
(T/F) Each line in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿

(T/F) If $$B = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ is a basis for a subspace $$H$$ of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then the correspondence $$\textbf{x}\mapsto\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$$ makes $$H$$ look and act the same as $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimension of Col $$A$$ is the number of pivot columns of $$A$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimension of Nul $$A$$ is the number of variables in the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimensions of Col $$A$$ and Nul $$A$$ add up to the number of columns of $$A$$ .﻿
(T/F) The dimension of the column space of $$A$$ is rank $$A$$ .﻿
(T/F) If a set of $$p$$ vectors spans a $$p$$ -dimensional subspace $$H$$ of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then these vectors form a basis for $$H$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$H$$ is a $$p$$ -dimensional subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then a linearly independent set of $$p$$ vectors in $$H$$ is a basis for $$H$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 27–32, justify each answer or construction.

problem.paragraph: If the subspace of all solutions of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has a basis consisting of three vectors and if $$A$$ is a $$5 \times 7$$ matrix, what is the rank of $$A$$ ?
What is the rank of a $$4 \times 5$$ matrix whose null space is three-dimensional?
If the rank of a $$7 \times 6$$ matrix $$A$$ is $$4$$ , what is the dimension of the solution space of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ ?

Show that a set of vectors $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{5}\}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is linearly dependent when dim Span $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{5}\} = 4$$ .﻿
If possible, construct a $$3 \times 4$$ matrix $$A$$ such that dim Nul $$A = 2$$ and dim Col $$A = 2$$ .
Construct a $$4 \times 3$$ matrix with rank $$l$$ .
Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times p$$ matrix whose column space is $$p$$ -dimensional. Explain why the columns of $$A$$ must be linearly independent.

Suppose columns $$1$$ , $$3$$ , $$5$$ , and $$6$$ of a matrix $$A$$ are linearly independent (but are not necessarily pivot columns) and the rank of $$A$$ is $$4$$ . Explain why the four columns mentioned must be a basis for the column space of $$A$$ .﻿

Suppose vectors $$\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{\textit{p}}$$ span a subspace $$W$$ , and let $$\{\textbf{a}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{a}_{\textit{q}}\}$$ be any set in $$W$$ containing more than $$p$$ vectors. Fill in the details of the following argument to show that $$\{\textbf{a}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{a}_{q}\}$$ must be linearly dependent. First, let $$B = \lbrack\textbf{b}_{1} \cdots \textbf{b}_{p}\rbrack$$ and $$A = \lbrack\textbf{a}_{1} \cdots \textbf{a}_{q}\rbrack$$ .﻿

list.item: Explain why for each vector $$\textbf{a}_{j},$$ there exists a vector $$\textbf{c}_{j}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ such that $$\textbf{a}_{j} = B\textbf{c}_{j}$$ .﻿
Let $$C = \lbrack\textbf{c}_{1} \cdots \textbf{c}_{q}\rbrack$$ . Explain why there is a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ such that $$C\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ .﻿
Use $$B$$ and $$C$$ to show that $$A\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ . This shows that the columns of $$A$$ are linearly dependent.

problem.paragraph: Use Exercise 35 to show that if $$A$$ and $$B$$ are bases for a subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then $$A$$ cannot contain more vectors than $$B$$ , and, conversely, $$B$$ cannot contain more vectors than $$A$$ .﻿

[T] Let $$H = \text{Span} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ and $$B = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ . Show that $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$H,$$ and find the $$\textit{B} \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ , when $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ - 5 \\ 10 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ - 8 \\ 13 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 \\ - 13 \\ 18 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}$$

[T] Let $$H = { \text{S} \text{p} \text{a} \text{n} }\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3}\}$$ and $$B = \left\{ {\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}} \right\}.$$ Show that $$B$$ is a basis for $$H$$ and $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$H$$ , and find the $$\textit{B} \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ , when $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 6 \\ 4 \\ - 9 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ - 3 \\ 7 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} - 9 \\ 5 \\ - 8 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 7 \\ - 8 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

problem.paragraph: Construct $$A = \lbrack\textbf{v}_{1} \textbf{v}_{2} \textbf{v}_{3}\rbrack$$ so that the subspace spanned by $$\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3}$$ is the column space of $$A$$ . A basis for this space is provided by the pivot columns of $$A$$ .﻿ $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & - 1 \\ - 8 & - 7 & 6 \\ 6 & - 1 & - 7 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & - 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & - 10 & - 4 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & - 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
The first two columns of $$A$$ are pivot columns and form a basis for $$H$$ . Thus $$\dim H = 2.$$

If $$\left\lbrack \textbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},$$ then $$\textbf{x}$$ is formed from a linear combination of the basis vectors using weights $$3$$ and $$2$$ : $$\textbf{x} = 3 \textbf{b}_{1} + 2 \textbf{b}_{2} = 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ .2 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \begin{bmatrix} .2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3.4 \\ 2.6 \end{bmatrix}$$

The basis $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2}\}$$ determines a coordinate system for $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ , illustrated by the grid in the figure. Note how $$\textbf{x}$$ is $$3$$ units in the $$\textbf{b}_{1} \text{-direction}$$ and $$2$$ units in the $$\textbf{b}_{2} \text{-direction}$$ .

A four-dimensional subspace would contain a basis of four linearly independent vectors. This is impossible inside $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}.$$ Since any linearly independent set in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ has no more than three vectors, any subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ has dimension no more than $$3$$ . The space $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ itself is the only three-dimensional subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ . Other subspaces of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ have dimension $$2$$ , $$1$$ , or $$0$$ .

section.heading: Chapter 2 Projects
section.paragraph: Chapter 2 projects are available online at bit.ly/30IM8gT.

list.item: Other Matrix Products: This project introduces two new operations on square matrices called the Jordan product and the commutator product and their properties are explored.
Adjacency Matrices: The purpose of this project is to show how powers of a matrix may be used to investigate graphs.
Dominance Matrices: The purpose of this project is to apply matrices and their powers to questions concerning various forms of competition between individuals and groups.

Condition Numbers: The purpose of this project is to show how a condition number of a matrix $$A$$ may be defined, and how its value affects the accuracy of solutions to systems of equations $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ .﻿

Equilibrium Temperature Distributions: The purpose of this project is to discuss a physical situation in which solving a system of linear equations becomes necessary: that of determining the equilibrium temperature of a thin plate.
The $$L U$$ and $$Q R$$ Factorizations: The purpose of this project is to explore a relationship between two matrix factorizations: the $$LU$$ factorization and the $$QR$$ factorization.
The Leontief Input–Output Model: The purpose of this project is to provide three more examples of the Leontief input–output model in action.
The Art of Linear Transformations: This project illustrates how to graph a polygon and then use linear transformations to move it around in the plane.

section.heading: Chapter 2 Supplementary Exercises
section.paragraph: Assume that the matrices mentioned in Exercises 1–15 below have appropriate sizes. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

list.item: (T/F) If $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$m \times n$$ , then both $$A B^{T}$$ and $$A^{T} B$$ are defined.
(T/F) If $$A B = C$$ and $$C$$ has $$2$$ columns, then $$A$$ has $$2$$ columns.
(T/F) Left-multiplying a matrix $$B$$ by a diagonal matrix $$A$$ , with nonzero entries on the diagonal, scales the rows of $$B$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$B C = B D$$ , then $$C = D$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$AC = 0$$ , then either $$A = 0$$ or $$C = 0$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$n \times n$$ , then $$(A + B)(A - B) = A^{2} - B^{2}$$ .﻿
(T/F) An elementary $$n \times n$$ matrix has either $$n$$ or $$n + 1$$ nonzero entries.
(T/F) The transpose of an elementary matrix is an elementary matrix.
(T/F) An elementary matrix must be square.
(T/F) Every square matrix is a product of elementary matrices.
(T/F) If $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix with three pivot positions, there exist elementary matrices $$E_{1},\ldots,E_{p}$$ such that $$E_{p}\cdots E_{1}A = I$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$A B = I$$ , then $$A$$ is invertible.
(T/F) If $$A$$ and $$B$$ are square and invertible, then $$A B$$ is invertible, and $$(A B)^{- 1} = A^{- 1}B^{- 1}$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$A B = B A$$ and if $$A$$ is invertible, then $$A^{- 1}B = B A^{- 1}$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$A$$ is invertible and if $$r \neq 0$$ , then $$(rA)^{- 1} = rA^{- 1}$$ .﻿
Find the matrix $$C$$ whose inverse is $$C^{- 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ .﻿
Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Show that $$A^{3} = 0$$ . Use matrix algebra to compute the product $$(I - A)(I + A + A^{2})$$ .﻿
Suppose $$A^{n} = 0$$ for some $$n > 1$$ . Find an inverse for $$I - A$$ .﻿
Suppose an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ satisfies the equation $$A^{2} - 2A + I = 0$$ . Show that $$A^{3} = 3A - 2I$$ and $$A^{4} = 4A - 3I$$ .﻿

Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 1 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ . These are Pauli spin matrices used in the study of electron spin in quantum mechanics. Show that $$A^{2} = I ,$$ $$B^{2} = I,$$ and $$A B = - B A$$ . Matrices such that $$A B = - B A$$ are said to anticommute.

Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 8 \\ 2 & 4 & {11} \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {- 3} & 5 \\ 1 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Compute $$A^{- 1}B$$ without computing $$A^{- 1}$$ . [Hint: $$A^{- 1}B$$ is the solution of the equation $$A X = B$$ .]

Find a matrix $$A$$ such that the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ maps $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ into $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},$$ respectively. [Hint: Write a matrix equation involving $$A,$$ and solve for $$A$$ .]
Suppose $$A B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5 & 4 \\ {- 2} & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$B = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Find $$A$$ .﻿
Suppose $$A$$ is invertible. Explain why $$A^{T} A$$ is also invertible. Then show that $$A^{- 1} = (A^{T} A)^{- 1}A^{T}$$ .﻿

Let $$x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ be fixed numbers. The matrix below, called a Vandermonde matrix, occurs in applications such as signal processing, error-correcting codes, and polynomial interpolation. $$V = \left[\right. 1 & x_{1} & x_{1}^{2} & \hdots & x_{1}^{n - 1} 1 & x_{2} & x_{2}^{2} & \hdots & x_{2}^{n - 1} \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots 1 & x_{n} & x_{n}^{2} & \hdots & x_{n}^{n - 1} \left]\right.$$ Given $$\textbf{y} = (y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , suppose $$\textbf{c} = (c_{0},\ldots,c_{n - 1})$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ satisfies $$V\textbf{c} = \textbf{y},$$ and define the polynomial $$p \left(\right. t \left.\right) = c_{0} + c_{1} t + c_{2} t^{2} + \hdots + c_{n - 1} t^{n - 1} .$$ Show that $$p(x_{1}) = y_{1},\ldots,p(x_{n}) = y_{n}$$ . We call $$p(t)$$ an interpolating polynomial for the points $$(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{n})$$ because the graph of $$p(t)$$ passes through the points. Suppose $$x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ are distinct numbers. Show that the columns of $$V$$ are linearly independent. [Hint: How many zeros can a polynomial of degree $$n - 1$$ have?] Prove: “If $$x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ are distinct numbers, and $$y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}$$ are arbitrary numbers, then there is an interpolating polynomial of degree $$\leq n - 1$$ for $$(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{n})$$ .”

Let $$A = L U$$ , where $$L$$ is an invertible lower triangular matrix and $$U$$ is upper triangular. Explain why the first column of $$A$$ is a multiple of the first column of $$L$$ . How is the second column of $$A$$ related to the columns of $$L$$ ?

Given $$\textbf{u}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ with $$\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{u} = 1,$$ let $$P = \textbf{uu}^{T}$$ (an outer product) and $$Q = I - 2P$$ . Justify statements $$(a)$$ , $$(b)$$ , and $$(c)$$ . $$P^{2} = P$$ $$P^{T} = P$$ $$Q^{2} = I$$ The transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto P\textbf{x}$$ is called a projection, and $$\textbf{x}\mapsto Q\textbf{x}$$ is called a Householder reflection. Such reflections are used in computer programs to create multiple zeros in a vector (usually a column of a matrix).

Let $$\textbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Determine $$P$$ and $$Q$$ as in Exercise 27, and compute $$P\textbf{x}$$ and $$Q\textbf{x}$$ . The figure shows that $$Q\textbf{x}$$ is the reflection of $$\textbf{x}$$ through the $$x_{1}x_{2} \text{-plane}$$ .

Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ singular matrix. Describe how to construct an $$n \times n$$ nonzero matrix $$B$$ such that $$A B = 0.$$
Let $$A$$ be a $$6 \times 4$$ matrix and $$B$$ a $$4 \times 6$$ matrix. Show that the $$6 \times 6$$ matrix $$A B$$ cannot be invertible.

[T] Certain dynamical systems can be studied by examining powers of a matrix, such as those below. Determine what happens to $$A^{k}$$ and $$B^{k}$$ as $$k$$ increases (for example, try $$k = 2,\ldots,16)$$ . Try to identify what is special about $$A$$ and $$B$$ . Investigate large powers of other matrices of this type, and make a conjecture about such matrices. $$A = \begin{bmatrix} .4 & .2 & .3 \\ .3 & .6 & .3 \\ .3 & .2 & .4 \end{bmatrix} , B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & .2 & .3 \\ .1 & .6 & .3 \\ .9 & .2 & .4 \end{bmatrix}$$

15. $$\text{Col} A = \mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , because $$A$$ has a pivot in each row, and so the columns of $$A$$ span $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . $$\text{Nul} A$$ cannot equal $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , because $$\text{Nul} A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{5}$$ . It is true, however, that $$\text{Nul} A$$ is two-dimensional. Reason: The equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has two free variables, because $$A$$ has five columns and only three of them are pivot columns.
17–25.See the Study Guide after you write your justifications.

27.The fact that the solution space of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has a basis of three vectors means that $$\dim \text{Nul} A = 3$$ . Since a $$5 \times 7$$ matrix $$A$$ has seven columns, the Rank Theorem shows that rank $$A = 7 - \dim \text{Nul} A = 4$$ . See the Study Guide for a justification that does not explicitly mention the Rank Theorem.

29.A $$7 \times 6$$ matrix has six columns. By the Rank Theorem, $$\dim \text{Nul} A = 6 - \text{rank} A$$ . Since the rank is four, $$\dim \text{Nul} A = 2$$ . That is, the dimension of the solution space of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ is two.

31.A $$3 \times 4$$ matrix $$A$$ with a two-dimensional column space has two pivot columns. The remaining two columns will correspond to free variables in the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ . So the desired construction is possible. There are six possible locations for the two pivot columns, one of which is $$\begin{bmatrix} \text{■} & \ast & \ast & \ast \\ 0 & \text{■} & \ast & \ast \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ . A simple construction is to take two vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that are obviously not linearly dependent and place them in a matrix along with a copy of each vector, in any order. The resulting matrix will obviously have a two-dimensional column space. There is no need to worry about whether $$\text{Nul} A$$ has the correct dimension, since this is guaranteed by the Rank Theorem: $$\dim \text{Nul} A = 4 - \text{rank} A$$ .

33.The $$p$$ columns of $$A$$ span $$\text{Col} A$$ by definition. If $$\dim \text{Col} A = p$$ , then the spanning set of $$p$$ columns is automatically a basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ , by the Basis Theorem. In particular, the columns are linearly independent.
